representative.quote: nature is so liberal to mankind, that, were all her presents equally divided among the species, and improved by art and industry, every individual would enjoy all the necessaries, and even most of the comforts of life; nor would ever be liable to any ills but such as might accidentally arise from the sickly frame and constitution of his body
representative.text: This is a strikingly optimistic view of nature's bounty and human potential. It sets up the ideal of perfect equality as something that could, in theory, provide for all. However, it also sets up the counterargument that Hume will later develop about the impracticality and potential harms of such equality.

representative.quote: were all her presents equally divided among the species, and improved by art and industry, every individual would enjoy all the necessaries, and even most of the comforts of life
representative.text: Hume sketches an almost utopian redistribution, assuming that technology can lift everyone to a baseline of comfort. The phrasing mirrors Enlightenment optimism about progress, yet he quickly turns to caution, signalling a tension between idealism and pragmatic skepticism.

representative.quote: and improved by art and industry
representative.text: The same faculty cuts both ways, and Hume never says what licenses the reversal. In paragraph one, nature's presents become "necessaries" and "comforts" only when "improved by art and industry" — industry is a condition of the ideal working. In paragraph two, differential "art, care, and industry" is the reason the ideal cannot hold. Unless the difference is purely temporal — a stock divided in one sentence, a flow in the next — the two paragraphs are not using the same premise. Note too that the second list adds a term the first lacks: "care." So the objection is not drawn from the first paragraph's premises at all; it introduces a new one about durable differences in disposition. That premise is what I press on in c9; here I only want to mark that it is a premise, not a restatement.

representative.quote: nor would ever be liable to any ills but such as might accidentally arise from the sickly frame and constitution of his body
representative.text: This clause quietly narrows the whole target. The equality Hume imagines is a rule about external possessions only; inequalities of body, health, and natural capacity are explicitly left in place, and treated as no objection at all (they are "accidental," a matter for the physician, not the legislator). So the phrase "PERFECT equality" is a misnomer from the start: what is under discussion is a distribution rule for goods, not for welfare or capacity. That makes the second paragraph's central objection strange. "Men's different degrees of art, care, and industry will immediately break that equality" is an argument from natural inequality — but Hume has already conceded natural inequality and found it unobjectionable, so it cannot by itself be the reason an equal distribution of *possessions* is impracticable. Unless he holds that we may leave natural inequality alone while forbidding its consequences in property, the moves sit badly together; he never says why the line falls there.

representative.quote: wherever we depart from this equality, we rob the poor of more satisfaction than we add to the rich
representative.text: This is the principle of diminishing marginal utility, stated outright about a century before the utilitarians worked it out formally. Hume grants it and never takes it back. Everything that follows is aimed at PERFECT equality, which is a narrower target than it first looks. Once he has conceded that every departure from equality costs the poor more than it gives the rich, his own standard ("most USEFUL and BENEFICIAL") seems to favour pushing toward equality as far as incentives and enforcement allow. The passage never asks where that point is.

representative.quote: wherever we depart from this equality, we rob the poor of more satisfaction than we add to the rich, and that the slight gratification of a frivolous vanity, in one individual, frequently costs more than bread to many families, and even provinces
representative.text: This passage highlights the moral argument for equality - that inequality creates disproportionate suffering for the poor compared to the benefits it provides to the rich. The vivid imagery of "frivolous vanity" costing "more than bread to many families" powerfully conveys the injustice of extreme inequality.

representative.quote: wherever we depart from this equality, we rob the poor of more satisfaction than we add to the rich
representative.text: This is a striking concession: the case against perfect equality has to outweigh a presumptive loss of satisfaction from inequality, not merely show that unequal outcomes reward merit.

representative.quote: the slight gratification of a frivolous vanity, in one individual, frequently costs more than bread to many families, and even provinces
representative.text: The passage's only quantifying image sits on the conceded side. Everything Hume says against perfect equality is institutional and abstract — inquisition, jurisdiction, tyranny, magistracy, subordination. The one concrete, human-scale comparison (a single vanity outweighing "bread to many families, and even provinces") belongs to the side he is about to defeat. Note the escalation from households to "provinces": it is the same scale argument that later reappears inverted in "the general INTEREST of mankind" — the unit of account quietly widens from the poorest household to the species as a whole, which is exactly what makes the opening concession dispensable. Also "frivolous vanity" marks his own position as a class judgment: it is not the rich person's legitimate consumption but his *vanity* whose cost is cited — the concession is granted about a contemptible motive, which subtly deflates it even as it is stated.

representative.quote: the rule of equality, as it would be highly USEFUL, is not altogether IMPRACTICABLE; but has taken place, at least in an imperfect degree, in some republics; particularly that of Sparta
representative.text: Hume acknowledges that some degree of equality has been achieved in certain societies, using Sparta as an example. However, he seems to view this as an imperfect and perhaps exceptional case rather than a broadly applicable model.

representative.quote: highly USEFUL, is not altogether IMPRACTICABLE
representative.text: The capitals are Hume's own emphatic capitalization, retained from his manuscript, not an editor's: USEFUL, IMPRACTICABLE, PERNICIOUS, BENEFICIAL, INTEREST are the load-bearing terms of the argument, and he marks them as such. Worth noticing that "USEFUL" appears on both sides of the pivot — equality would be "highly USEFUL" in his own concession, and the rules he defends must be "most USEFUL" — so the word is doing dialectical work, not simply the work of a utilitarian slogan.

representative.quote: particularly that of Sparta; where it was attended, it is said, with the most beneficial consequences
representative.text: Two things here. First, the hedge "it is said" — Hume defers to report rather than asserting Sparta's success himself, which is characteristically careful for a man who elsewhere (in the History) is less charitable about Lycurgus. Second, a historical irony: Spartan equality was institutional — the kleroi were inalienable, no trading of land permitted. So the one case he names as working at "an imperfect degree" worked precisely by suppressing the third principle he endorses in the last paragraph, "That it may be alienated by consent." The imperfect equality that succeeded did so by abolishing one of the rules he calls useful.

representative.quote: the Agrarian laws, so frequently claimed in Rome, and carried into execution in many Greek cities, proceeded, all of them, from a general idea of the utility of this principle.
representative.text: Hume treats the ‘Agrarian laws’ as a uniform illustration of egalitarian policy, but historically these reforms were highly varied and often driven by political expediency rather than a principled belief in equality. By grouping Rome and diverse Greek poleis together, he glosses over the fact that many of these measures (e.g., the Roman agraria of the Gracchi) were contested precisely because they threatened entrenched property rights, which Hume later defends. The passage thus shows a selective use of history to bolster his argument that equality has already found practical expression, even though the cases are more nuanced.

representative.quote: the Agrarian laws, so frequently claimed in Rome, and carried into execution in many Greek cities, proceeded, all of them, from a general idea of the utility of this principle.
representative.text: The inference is asked to bear more than the evidence can. The Roman agrarian laws concerned the occupation of public land, not the levelling of all possessions; they were partisan measures, repeatedly defeated and eventually fatal to their sponsors. Reading them as testimony to a shared sense of equality's utility converts contested class legislation into consensus. This matters because paragraph two discards the same evidence by the same gesture — "historians... may inform us" — without saying what in the record he now weighs differently (c23).

representative.quote: But historians, and even common sense, may inform us, that, however specious these ideas of PERFECT equality may seem, they are really, at bottom, IMPRACTICABLE
representative.text: Notice that the tribunal changes between the paragraphs. Paragraph one argues from confessed premises; paragraph two appeals to "historians, and even common sense." But the historians are the same witnesses. The Sparta and the Roman agrarian laws that made equality look practicable a few lines earlier came from exactly this source, and Hume does not say which reading of the record is the sound one — he simply re-cites authority with the sign reversed. An empiricist's argument should have to tell us what in the historical evidence decides it; otherwise "historians may inform us" is a gesture toward a verdict, not a report of one.

representative.quote: however specious these ideas of PERFECT equality may seem, they are really, at bottom, IMPRACTICABLE; and were they not so, would be extremely PERNICIOUS to human society
representative.text: This is the crux of Hume's argument against perfect equality. He contends that it is not only impractical to achieve, but would actually be harmful to society if it could be achieved. This sets up his reasoning about the necessity of inequality for motivating productivity and maintaining social order.

representative.quote: Render possessions ever so equal, men's different degrees of art, care, and industry will immediately break that equality. Or if you check these virtues, you reduce society to the most extreme indigence
representative.text: Hume argues that human differences in skill, effort, and diligence will inevitably create inequality, even if possessions start out equal. Trying to suppress these differences, he contends, would stifle the virtues that drive economic productivity and lead to widespread poverty.

representative.quote: Render possessions ever so equal, men's different degrees of art, care, and industry will immediately break that equality. Or if you check these virtues, you reduce society to the most extreme indigence
representative.text: The alternatives move quickly from unequal rewards to checking the virtues themselves. Redistribution could leave differences in reward without enforcing perfect equality; the argument against the latter does not settle how much inequality is useful.

representative.quote: men's different degrees of art, care, and industry will immediately break that equality
representative.text: The load-bearing premise of the whole reversal. It is a regularity claim about how people actually behave, not a claim about what is owed — and it is doing all the work. Note the shape of the argument: any attempt to hold the equality in place must "check these virtues," which lowers total product. That is the levelling-down objection in its modern form. But the premise is empirical and contestable; the Sparta reference in the preceding paragraph cuts the other way, and Hume offers nothing for "immediately" beyond assertion. If the dispositions are even partly endogenous to institutions, the premise is circular: arrangements that reward differential industry produce differential industry, and then get cited as proof that equality cannot survive.

representative.quote: The most rigorous inquisition too is requisite to watch every inequality on its first appearance; and the most severe jurisdiction, to punish and redress it
representative.text: Hume points out the practical challenges of enforcing perfect equality. It would require constant surveillance and harsh punishments to maintain, which he implies would be tyrannical and partial.

representative.quote: But besides, that so much authority must soon degenerate into tyranny, and be exerted with great partialities; who can possibly be possessed of it, in such a situation as is here supposed?
representative.text: This is a neat dilemma, and it's easy to read past. Keeping equality in place needs a great concentration of power. But a society with equal possessions has, by Hume's lights, nothing to support that power, because authority grows out of subordination and subordination grows out of unequal property. So the enforcer either can't exist, or exists only because a new inequality (of power instead of goods) has appeared, which defeats the point. The final sentence ("reduce all power nearly to a level, as well as property") is the second horn of that dilemma.

representative.quote: who can possibly be possessed of it, in such a situation as is here supposed?
representative.text: This is the structural objection, not merely the practical one. The enforcing authority presupposes the very subordination the regime destroys: "Perfect equality of possessions, destroying all subordination, weakens extremely the authority of magistracy, and must reduce all power nearly to a level, as well as property." It's a bootstrapping failure — the policeman of equality is himself an agent in the society equality levels, so the mechanism is dissolved before it can operate. The "most rigorous inquisition" demanded in the previous sentence is demanded by a power that the doctrine simultaneously annuls.

representative.quote: Perfect equality of possessions, destroying all subordination, weakens extremely the authority of magistracy, and must reduce all power nearly to a level, as well as property
representative.text: Hume argues that perfect equality would undermine social hierarchies and the authority of government. Without inequality of property and power, he suggests, there would be no basis for the subordination necessary to maintain social order.

representative.quote: in order to establish laws for the regulation of property, we must be acquainted with the nature and situation of man; must reject appearances, which may be false, though specious; and must search for those rules, which are, on the whole, most USEFUL and BENEFICIAL
representative.text: Hume advocates for a pragmatic approach to property laws, based on an understanding of human nature and aimed at promoting overall utility and benefit to society, rather than pursuing an unrealistic ideal of perfect equality.

representative.quote: Vulgar sense and slight experience are sufficient for this purpose; where men give not way to too selfish avidity, or too extensive enthusiasm.
representative.text: A nice closing couplet of vices. "Too selfish avidity" is the greed that over-claims for the individual; "too extensive enthusiasm" is the zeal that over-claims for the abstract principle — here, perfect equality. The passage has just spent itself warning against enthusiasm for the specious ideal, and closes by naming both distortions of judgment about property. Note "enthusiasm" is 18th-century *zeal*, with its residual religious taint, not mere interest. Also "specious" has done its work twice in the passage ("however specious these ideas … may seem" / "may be false, though specious") — it is the hinge-word of the whole argument: appearances are conceded, then rejected, on practical rather than moral grounds.

representative.quote: Vulgar sense and slight experience are sufficient for this purpose; where men give not way to too selfish avidity, or too extensive enthusiasm.
representative.text: Consider what common sense is being asked to certify: Sparta, the Roman agrarian laws, a conjecture about incentives, and then inheritance, alienation, and the bindingness of contract — all delivered as self-evident under "Who sees not." But the same vulgar sense produced the specious appearance in paragraph one; the whole function of that paragraph is to show that the plausible reading is the wrong one. So "vulgar sense and slight experience" cannot be the operative standard, or the passage refutes itself. The real criterion is "on the whole" — a system-level utility test — and Hume asserts that partial equalization fails it rather than showing it. Also note that "enthusiasm" is the word for the leveller: the last sentence is a boundary-drawing move, not an argument.

representative.quote: Who sees not, for instance, that whatever is produced or improved by a man's art or industry ought, for ever, to be secured to him
representative.text: The four “Who sees not...?” clauses do more than list rules: they perform the argument. By framing each principle as something obvious to “vulgar sense,” Hume makes dissent seem perverse rather than reasoned. The device mirrors the earlier dismissal of “too extensive enthusiasm” — the rhetorical questions are an appeal to moderation itself, inviting the reader to feel that only a zealot could deny what “everyone sees.” Note too the progression: labor (individual production) → inheritance (family time) → alienation (market exchange) → contract (social framework). Each step widens the circle of cooperation, so that by the end “the general INTEREST of mankind” sounds like the natural culmination of common observation rather than a theoretical conclusion. The form disguises the radical conventionalism: these are not natural rights discovered by reason, but conventions whose “obviousness” is a product of long habituation — precisely the kind of “slight experience” the closing couplet praises.

representative.quote: whatever is produced or improved by a man's art or industry ought, for ever, to be secured to him, in order to give encouragement to such USEFUL habits and accomplishments
representative.text: This encapsulates Hume's view that property rights are necessary to incentivize productive behavior. By securing to individuals the fruits of their labor, society encourages habits and accomplishments that are useful to all.

representative.quote: That the property ought also to descend to children and relations, for the same USEFUL purpose?
representative.text: “For the same” compresses an additional argument. Securing a producer's own enjoyment and securing a relative's inheritance need not encourage industry to the same extent; inherited wealth may also weaken the recipient's incentive to work. The relevant question, on Hume's own test, is the net effect of a particular inheritance rule, not whether inheritance simply follows from the case for rewarding production.

representative.quote: That the property ought also to descend to children and relations, for the same USEFUL purpose?
representative.text: "The same USEFUL purpose" covers a gap. Securing what a person produces encourages that person's own industry. Inheritance hands the heir something they did not work for. It can only encourage the parent's industry, as a motive to keep earning for one's family, and it may well dull the heir's. So the argument may still go through, but it's a different argument from the first one, and the rhetorical questions ("Who sees not...?") are carrying more weight here than anywhere else in the list.

representative.quote: the property ought also to descend to children and relations, for the same USEFUL purpose? That it may be alienated by consent, in order to beget that commerce and intercourse, which is so BENEFICIAL to human society? And that all contracts and promises ought carefully to be fulfilled, in order to secure mutual trust and confidence, by which the general INTEREST of mankind is so much promoted
representative.text: Hume outlines the key features of a property system that he believes will promote social utility: inheritance, voluntary exchange, and the enforcement of contracts. These, he argues, create the conditions for beneficial commerce and the trust necessary for cooperation.

representative.quote: That it may be alienated by consent, in order to beget that commerce and intercourse, which is so BENEFICIAL to human society?
representative.text: The third rule — alienability by consent — is the hinge between the first two (production/inheritance, which secure the *supply* side of prosperity) and the fourth (contract, which secures the *trust* side). Without alienation, property is a dead stock; with it, property becomes circulating capital. Hume's "BENEFICIAL" here is distinctly commercial: the gain isn't just more goods but the *intercourse* itself — the social fabric of exchange. This connects to c12's irony about Sparta: the one historical case Hume cites of "imperfect equality" working *suppressed* this very rule (kleroi were inalienable). So the regime that approached his conceded ideal did so by blocking the mechanism he now calls essential to utility. The passage's own logic suggests Sparta's equality was stable precisely because it wasn't a commercial society — it bought equality at the cost of the "intercourse" Hume treats as a primary benefit.

representative.quote: And that all contracts and promises ought carefully to be fulfilled, in order to secure mutual trust and confidence, by which the general INTEREST of mankind is so much promoted?
representative.text: The fourth rhetorical question shifts the justification from production and exchange to social cohesion itself. Where security of labor and inheritance encourage industry, and alienation encourages commerce, contract-keeping secures the "mutual trust" that underwrites both. Note that "INTEREST" is capitalized here (like USEFUL and BENEFICIAL before), but it is explicitly collective — "of mankind" — not merely the aggregated private advantage. The arc of the four rules thus moves from the individual (secure my labor) to the family (inheritance) to the market (alienation) to the common framework of expectation. This completes Hume's replacement of distributive justice with a systemic, conventionalist account: property laws are justified not by who deserves what, but by the interdependent social order they make possible.

representative.quote: The laws and conditions of the Production of Wealth partake of the character of physical truths. There is nothing optional or arbitrary in them. It is not so with the Distribution of Wealth.
representative.text: The famous hinge, and easy to misread if you stop at the first two sentences. Mill is not saying production is nature and distribution is pure will. He is saying the *choice* of distributive rules is institutional, while both the laws of production and the *consequences* of whatever rules you choose have the character of physical truths. The sentence two beats later — consequences "are as little arbitrary... as the laws of production" — is the real methodological claim. Read alone, the opening invites the criticism that what gets produced depends on who is paid to produce it. Mill knows that feedback; he is licensing a separate analysis of distribution, not denying the loop.

representative.quote: The laws and conditions of the Production of Wealth partake of the character of physical truths. There is nothing optional or arbitrary in them. It is not so with the Distribution of Wealth. That is a matter of human institution solely.
representative.text: Mill's distinction between production and distribution is foundational to his political economy. By framing production as governed by immutable physical laws, he creates a stark contrast with distribution, which he presents as entirely malleable through human institutions and social choices. This sets the stage for his analysis of property as a social construct rather than a natural law.

representative.quote: The laws and conditions of the Production of Wealth partake of the character of physical truths. There is nothing optional or arbitrary in them. It is not so with the Distribution of Wealth.
representative.text: Worth noticing how much the argument depends on how hard this line is drawn. "Physical truths" cannot mean that production is independent of human choice — it plainly depends on labour, skill, and the decision to work at all. The claim must be about constraint rather than causation: given the resources and techniques available, nature fixes what can be produced, while no such constraint fixes who gets it. So the dichotomy is really between the feasible set and the choice of a point within it. That is a defensible distinction, but it is a distinction about limits, and it leaves open how much of observed production is itself fixed by distribution rules — a question the next paragraph's method quietly sets aside.

representative.quote: The laws and conditions of the Production of Wealth partake of the character of physical truths.
representative.text: A caveat about the text we are all parsing: this is a Laughlin abridgement of the *Principles*, and the opening of Mill's paragraph, as I remember it, goes on past this sentence to name the constraints — that whatever is produced must be produced in the modes and under the conditions imposed by the constitution of external things and by the bodily and mental structure of the producers — before arriving at "whether they like it or not." If that is right, the abridgement keeps the conclusion and drops the premise that specified it, and the claim then circulates as an axiom rather than as the summary of a stated argument. That is precisely the shape the objections in this margin keep pressing on. Worth checking against the full text by anyone who has it; and if the scissors fell here, it is worth asking where else.

representative.quote: It is not so with the Distribution of Wealth. That is a matter of human institution solely.
representative.text: Mill’s insistence that distribution is "solely" a matter of human institution seems to ignore the way institutional constraints (e.g., property rights, power structures) shape what choices are actually possible, making the space of ‘human‑made’ rules already bounded by existing material conditions.

representative.quote: The things once there, mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like.
representative.text: The whole production/distribution split depends on "once there." It treats production as finished before distribution starts. But people produce with an expectation of how the product will be shared. Change the rules of distribution and you change what gets produced, how much, and by whom. Mill half-concedes this two sentences later, when he says the *consequences* of distributive rules are as law-like as production. Some of those consequences land back on production, though. So distribution can't be "optional" in the strong sense he first claims. It is optional only once, at the moment the rule is chosen. After that the rule is bound by consequences that work like physical laws.

representative.quote: what the opinions and feelings of the ruling portion of the community make them
representative.text: Watch the subject change mid-sentence. The rules "are what the opinions and feelings of the ruling portion of the community make them" — a frank concession that distribution expresses power, not consensus — yet they "might be still more different, if mankind so chose." Who chooses? If rules track the ruling portion, altering them requires either the rulers' feelings to shift or the rulers to be replaced; "mankind" as such has no lever to pull. Mill slides from something close to a sociology of class rule into a voluntarist idiom within a single breath, and seems not to feel the seam. Later socialists made this the crux: distribution is not chosen but imposed. Mill concedes the premise while keeping the irenic grammar of choice.

representative.quote: The things once there, mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like.
representative.text: "Once there" is doing quiet work. It freezes the stock so that the question of who may have it can be asked apart from how it came to exist. That is a permission to proceed, not a finding that incentives, saving, and labor supply are indifferent to the rules. The phrase is what later readers either lean on or indict.

representative.quote: mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like. They can place them at the disposal of whomsoever they please, and on whatever terms.
representative.text: "Individually or collectively" is not emphasis. A bequest and a tax are the same kind of act in this sentence: someone placing things at another's disposal, on terms. Nothing marks individual disposition as the undesigned baseline and collective disposition as the interference. That anti-naturalizing move has to be in place before private property can appear as one arrangement among others rather than as the fact from which distribution departs. "On whatever terms" widens the grant from who receives the stock to the conditions of the placing — sale, gift, allotment, succession — which is the license Mill later uses when inheritance and the terms of landholding turn out to be revisable without his abandoning the institution.

representative.quote: mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like
representative.text: The phrase multiplies the forms of *holding* while leaving the production side in the singular: wealth turns up here without a producer. Had the same latitude been extended backwards — had "individually or collectively" also described who works, who owns the means, and on what terms — the distribution question would already have swallowed the production question, which is why the freedom is granted only to the hand reaching into the heap and never to the process that filled it. Same closure as c40, seen from the other end: there the cast of claimants is given before the rule is chosen; here the modes of possession are declared free while the process generating the thing possessed is left in a grammar with no subject.

representative.quote: can do with them as they like
representative.text: One boundary the frame never draws: disposal by whom, over what, and against whom. "Mankind... collectively" is a bounded people and "the things once there" is a stock already inside the boundary; the paragraph has no term for what is not yet there. But the century that wrote it was steadily moving things inside the boundary — enclosure at home (c33, c39), dispossession and fresh land abroad — and each such act is a distribution performed on parties who are not in the room and not part of the "mankind" whose choosing this sentence makes its subject. The tribunal's clock-starting (c4) is the domestic form of the same device: the rule begins once possession is settled, and neither court nor theory is given anything to say about the turning-out that settled it. A distribution fixed at the frontier is, on this paragraph's own terms, as much a matter of human institution as any other — and, for the same reason, equally invisible.

representative.quote: They can place them at the disposal of whomsoever they please, and on whatever terms.
representative.text: "Whomsoever" and "whatever terms" are not the same concession. Who receives the stock is an allocation; the terms are the conditions of the transfer — wage, rent, term of years, liability, tax. It is the second that walks straight back into the next period's production. Mill's own sentence already holds the feedback that "once there" seems to have closed: you may set any terms you like, and the terms then set how much labor and land are offered. The physical-law character he restores to consequences gets its purchase here, not in a later hedge. Readers who stop at the liberty of disposal are reading half the clause.

representative.quote: on whatever terms
representative.text:
Easy to read past: not just *to whom*, but *on what terms*. Shares are one dimension of distribution; terms are another — tenure, lease, entail, inheritance, revocability. The phrase quietly claims for "mankind" a design-space much larger than reallocating a stock: the whole law of holding is up for revision. And it is the dimension Book II actually works in. Its real comparisons — peasant proprietor versus cottier, métayage versus the English farm system — are differences of terms: the same land, the same laborer, different conditions of holding. The pie-slicing picture invited by "the things once there" is already obsolete three sentences later.
(see also: c18, c40)

representative.quote: The Distribution of Wealth depends on the laws and customs of society.
representative.text: Note that Mill says "laws and customs", not laws alone. Since custom and moral opinion are part of the distributive machinery, the lever of reform is not only legislation but changing opinion — which the next sentence names in the "opinions and feelings of the ruling portion". This also fits the methodological pivot: distributive rules are conventional and changeable, but they are embedded in custom as much as in statute, so they can only be changed through the community's "opinions and feelings", not by a bare act of will.

representative.quote: and might be still more different, if mankind so chose
representative.text: The previous sentence named the actual rule-maker — "the ruling portion"; this clause hands the choice to "mankind." Mill alternates between the two subjects within three sentences, and the reform enterprise of Book II lives in the alternation: since rules are made of "opinions and feelings," they can be remade by changing opinions — which is what this very book is for. Political economy doubles as a technique for editing the feelings of the ruling portion. And note the comparative tucked into the conditional: "still more different." Actual history is not the full menu of the possible.

representative.quote: and are very different in different ages and countries; and might be still more different, if mankind so chose.
representative.text:
Mill's evidence for the conventionality of distribution is comparative variety, and variety is weaker evidence than the claim he needs. Two societies may differ because their opinions differ, or because their conditions differ and each rule is the fitting response to its own conditions; the record cannot discriminate between those. So the descriptive premise supports at most the contingency of *these* rules, while "might be still more different, if mankind so chose" is a claim about a counterfactual space the comparative record never samples. The sentence gets its force from an unearned slide from variety to plasticity. Mill needs plasticity rather than arbitrariness (as c8 argues), but the passage does not argue for plasticity directly — it infers a modal claim from an inductive one. What would license it is a mechanism: rules made by opinions and feelings that could have been otherwise. That mechanism is supplied, and only piecemeal, two paragraphs later in the tribunal story.
(see also: c8, c17)

representative.quote: might be still more different, if mankind so chose
representative.text: Mill inserts a conditional that re‑opens the space of collective agency: the distribution rules could be reshaped arbitrarily by ‘mankind’. Yet he immediately nests this agency in the ‘ruling portion of the community’ (c14, c20), exposing a tension between a democratic ideal and the reality of elite control. The phrase thus functions as a rhetorical hedge – it invites reformist optimism while quietly delimiting the horizon of change to the preferences of those who already hold power.

representative.quote: might be still more different, if mankind so chose
representative.text: The margin's busiest thread — the seam c19 found between class rule and voluntarism, worked over by c23, c24, c29, c32 — may be arguing across a text that is missing its hinge. In the full Principles, if memory serves, the very next sentences after "if mankind so chose" run: "The opinions and feelings of mankind, doubtless, are not a matter of chance. They are consequences of the fundamental laws of human nature, combined with the existing state of knowledge and experience, and the existing condition of social institutions and intellectual and moral culture." Mill does feel the seam; he pins it. Choosing is itself caused. That concedes c32's diagnosis — opinions are the lever — and then specifies the only mechanism he believes in: knowledge, experience, moral culture, i.e. slow causation (the ethological program of the Logic, Book VI), not will. So "if mankind so chose" is second-order voluntarism: what is optional is whether a generation that understands this works on the antecedents — which is also the precise sense in which this book aims at the causal variable (c41). Worth verifying against an unabridged text; after c37, every seam we find in this excerpt now invites that check.

representative.quote: We have here to consider, not the causes, but the consequences, of the rules according to which wealth may be distributed. Those, at least, are as little arbitrary, and have as much the character of physical laws, as the laws of production.
representative.text: And here Mill immediately takes back half of the freedom he just granted! You can choose any rule of distribution you please, he says, *but* once you choose the rule, its consequences follow with the necessity of physical law. This is how he reconciles radical openness about institutions (like socialism or cooperative ownership) with strict classical economic determinism about incentives, population, and capital accumulation.

representative.quote: We have here to consider, not the causes, but the consequences, of the rules according to which wealth may be distributed.
representative.text: A jurisdiction rule: causes off the docket, consequences on. Then the next two paragraphs are almost entirely genealogy — tribunals, first occupancy, rude ages. This is not a lapse. Causes are disclaimed as *explanation* and retained as *rhetoric*: an origin story can discredit a natural-right claim (whatever our property came from, it was not desert or contract) while carrying no normative weight in either direction. Consequences are then left holding the entire justificatory load — which is precisely why Mill has to insist, in the preceding sentence, that they are as hard as physical law. A soft consequence claim would leave property at once unjustified by its past and unconstrained in its effects, and the utilitarian apology for it would have nothing to stand on.

representative.quote: We have here to consider, not the causes, but the consequences, of the rules according to which wealth may be distributed. Those, at least, are as little arbitrary, and have as much the character of physical laws, as the laws of production.
representative.text: Notice how quickly the door that was just flung open is narrowed again. Society may choose the rules arbitrarily, yet the *consequences* of any chosen rule snap right back into the realm of quasi-physical necessity. Freedom enters only at the legislative threshold; one step across it, natural law resumes jurisdiction. Political economy thus shifts from proclaiming "there is only one system" to presenting a menu of institutional options with determinate, non-negotiable price tags attached to each.

representative.quote: We have here to consider, not the causes, but the consequences, of the rules according to which wealth may be distributed.
representative.text: This is the methodological hinge of the whole Book, and it is a truncation rather than a finding. Causes are bracketed; consequences become the tribunal. It is a coherent Benthamite move — the rules were made by "opinions and feelings," so arguing about their pedigree is idle; ask instead what they produce. But the bracketing is expensive. Which consequences follow from a rule depends on the circumstances that produced the rule, so the two questions are not cleanly separable, and the reformer who ignores causes will keep rediscovering them as obstacles.

representative.quote: the different modes of distributing the produce of land and labor, which have been adopted in practice, or may be conceived in theory
representative.text:
This announcement — practice and theory both admitted, no mode excluded in advance — is the freest line in the passage, and the next sentence surrenders much of it ("first claimed by" individual property). But a subtler closure sits inside the line itself. What is to be distributed is "the produce of land and labor": the claimants are already given before any rule is chosen. The advertised freedom is freedom to fix the *terms* among a fixed cast of claimants; whether the cast itself — who counts as a producer, whether labor is a factor or a relation — is institutional never comes up. Same closing move as "once there," one level down: not only is the heap given, so are the number and names of the hands reaching into it.
(see also: c8, c9)

representative.quote: the different modes of distributing the produce of land and labor, which have been adopted in practice, or may be conceived in theory
representative.text: Two setups in one sentence. (1) "or may be conceived in theory" is the warrant for the chapter's later, notably fair hearing of socialist schemes: the object of enquiry is conceivable distributive orders, not historical ones — consistent with the first paragraph's rule of weighing rules by consequences rather than origin. (2) "Land and labor" is a classical two-factor shorthand, not an oversight: in this system the return to stock is not a third produce of production but a deduction from what labour produces (rent being a deduction from what land produces). So the elementary distributional questions are rent and wages, with profits entering as a claim on labour's produce. That is also why the next paragraph's origin story can be told entirely in terms of possession of things — land, movables — rather than title to capital: the "primary and fundamental" property in view is property in land and in the product of one's own labour.

representative.quote: which have been adopted in practice, or may be conceived in theory
representative.text: A quiet charter for the next two chapters. Existing institutions and merely-conceivable ones are admitted on equal footing as objects of analysis — the space of the conceivable exceeds the space of the tried — and that parity is what lets Mill put communism on the dissecting table beside property, as a comparator rather than a crime or a chimera. The method is already a politics: to enumerate the alternatives neutrally is to have relativized the status quo. What later readers call Mill's wavering between property and socialism is licensed right here, in a subordinate clause.

representative.quote: which have been adopted in practice, or may be conceived in theory
representative.text: Three words license utopia as an object of economic science: "conceived in theory." In 1848 the inventory of alternatives "adopted in practice" is thin — sectarian communities, Owenite fragments, the "exceptional and very limited cases" just acknowledged — so the theoretical space must do nearly all the comparative work. And it can do that work only because of the hinge two sentences back: untried institutions are evaluable only if their consequences are lawlike and therefore predictable. Theory substitutes for experiment. The comparative chapters that follow — communism, peasant proprietorship, the probable future of the labouring classes — are this sentence carried out, and their claim to be science rather than wishful thinking stands or falls with c19's hinge.

representative.quote: though in its secondary features it has varied, and is liable to vary
representative.text: This hedge does a lot of work and has had no comment yet. Mill calls individual property "primary and fundamental", which reassures readers, and in the same breath makes its "secondary features" variable. Neither side of that line is drawn here. Later in the book he places bequest, land ownership, and the size of inheritances on the variable side. So "fundamental" turns out to mean something like "some form of exclusive individual holding", not the property law of 1848. Whatever reform programme the book has largely depends on how much he can move from the first category into the second.

representative.quote: that primary and fundamental institution, on which, unless in some exceptional and very limited cases, the economical arrangements of society have always rested, though in its secondary features it has varied, and is liable to vary
representative.text: The freedom announced a few lines earlier — rules "might be still more different, if mankind so chose" — is spent before it is used. Variation is conceded only in "secondary features"; anything not resting on individual property is filed as "exceptional and very limited," so that "always" can still be said. Plasticity survives for inheritance, tenure, the terms on which the produce is handed over. It does not survive for the institution that frames those terms. "Primary and fundamental" does the same quiet work as "once there": it freezes a background so that what remains looks like reform of an arrangement rather than choice among arrangements. Nothing yet argued has made that background the obvious one. The "of course" in the next sentence is doing the choosing.

representative.quote: unless in some exceptional and very limited cases, the economical arrangements of society have always rested, though in its secondary features it has varied, and is liable to vary. I mean, of course, the institution of individual property.
representative.text: Three things work quietly here. (1) "I mean, of course": in the year of revolutions, the studied casualness names as obvious the institution the chapter will shortly weigh even-handedly against communism. The "of course" is a courtesy extended to the reader, not a premise the argument relies on. (2) The primary/secondary architecture offers a way out of the tension c7 notes between the tribunal parenthesis ("always precede laws") and the opening voluntarism: the peacekeeping ratification of possession is the invariant kernel; what varies with "the opinions and feelings of the ruling portion" is the superstructure — what counts as possession, inheritance, tenures, remedies. That steadies the rhetoric more than the theory, since the kernel is anything but distributionally innocent (c4's clock point), but it does make the chapter's three paragraphs cohere. (3) "Exceptional and very limited cases" is the clause communism will come through. Between the first edition (1848) and the third (1852) Mill rewrote this chapter's treatment of socialism from stated opposition into the famous near-even balance — communism measured against the actual, not the ideal, working of property, its difficulties as "dust in the balance" — a rewriting the Autobiography describes as growing out of study and discussion with Harriet Taylor Mill. Laughlin's abridgement drops almost all of that material, so a reader of this text sees the door but not the room it opened into.

representative.quote: that primary and fundamental institution, on which, unless in some exceptional and very limited cases, the economical arrangements of society have always rested
representative.text: Note the tension with the following paragraph: here the institution is "primary and fundamental" and has "always" supported society's arrangements; a few lines later its actual origin is a contingent default rule of early tribunals, ungrounded in justice or utility. The "always rested" claim is doing enormous work — it is the premise the chapter's conservatism depends on, and it sits uneasily beside the origin story.

representative.quote: unless in some exceptional and very limited cases, the economical arrangements of society have always rested
representative.text: The exception clause is a device with a precise logic: name the counterexamples in advance and file them under "exceptional and very limited," and you buy the universal "always" at a price you have already agreed to pay. What gets filed away is not this or that community but the *possibility of a system* — an economy whose arrangements do not rest on individual property in any of its secondary shapes. An exception conceded in advance can never afterwards be produced as evidence against the rule; it has already been counted and assigned its weight, which is nil. And the clause is unargued: no case cited, no criterion offered for "very limited," no reason given why the exceptions could not be the interesting cases. It is the same move as the "of course" two sentences later — a place where the reader's assent is assumed in order to secure a claim that is never defended.

representative.quote: I mean, of course, the institution of individual property.
representative.text:
Two tells in one sentence. "Of course" locates the audience: readers for whom individual property is the default setting of the world — the propertied English reader, two paragraphs after being told distribution "might be still more different, if mankind so chose." Mill starts where his reader is, not where his argument is. And note the word is "individual," not "private": he needs the term that has an antonym. "Individual property" already implies common or joint property as its coordinate alternative, so the comparison that will occupy the rest of the chapter is embedded in the vocabulary before any institution has been examined. "Private" would smuggle in exclusion as definitional; "individual" leaves the rule of holding open.
(see also: c22, c38)

representative.quote: Private property, as an institution, did not owe its origin to any of those considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established.
representative.text: A vital methodological distinction between historical genealogy and normative justification. Against the Lockean or natural-rights tradition, which tends to mythologize the origin of property (mixing one's labor with the soil in a state of nature) in order to sanctify it, Mill cheerfully concedes that property began as a crude peace-keeping expedient: freezing the status quo of possession simply to stop people from hitting each other. Its justification for *continuing* to exist has to rest on current utility, not ancient pedigree.

representative.quote: Enough is known of rude ages, both from history and from analogous states of society in our own time
representative.text: A methodological claim that goes almost unnoticed: the evidence for this genealogy is "history" plus "analogous states of society in our own time." Mill treats contemporary societies he regards as rude as living specimens of an earlier stage, so that ethnography can stand in for a missing archive. That lets him speak with confidence about what tribunals "originally" did. It also imports a ranking — some present societies are the past of others — and whatever those observers happened to count as occupancy becomes the universal origin of property. The bright line he describes may be as much a feature of the analogy as of the tribunals.

representative.quote: tribunals (which always precede laws) were originally established, not to determine rights, but to repress violence and terminate quarrels. With this object chiefly in view, they naturally enough gave legal effect to first occupancy, by treating as the aggressor the person who first commenced violence, by turning, or attempting to turn, another out of possession.
representative.text: A quiet replacement of Locke by Hume. First occupancy gets legal effect not because labor mixed with the world confers title, but because courts exist to stop fights, and protecting the possessor is the cheapest peacekeeping rule available: the challenger is legible as "the aggressor." Property is thus born as a byproduct of violence-suppression and only afterward acquires its utilitarian apology ("considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established"). Two consequences Mill fully intends: origin cannot sanctify the institution (no natural right here), but neither can origin damn it — justification is relocated entirely into present consequences, which is exactly the ground from which Book II will later put the institution itself on trial. There is also something darker, said blandly: a rule that protects whoever is in possession ratifies possession however acquired, and punishes only the second act of violence, never the first. The original taking sits outside the frame; the tribunal's jurisdiction begins by freezing it in place.

representative.quote: tribunals (which always precede laws) were originally established, not to determine rights, but to repress violence and terminate quarrels
representative.text: "Tribunals (which always precede laws)" — Mill inverts the standard Hobbesian/Lockean story where law creates the tribunal. Here, adjudication of disputes (ending violence) comes first; codified rights follow. Property emerges as a peacekeeping device, not a natural right.

representative.quote: tribunals (which always precede laws)
representative.text: This parenthesis is easy to pass over, but the argument in the next clause depends on it. If people settled disputes before they wrote rules, then property law grew out of rulings on particular quarrels, not from a principle laid down first. That is why first occupancy can come in "naturally enough": it is the rule that falls out of a judge's practical problem (who started this?), not a conclusion anyone reasoned to. Two observations. First, "always" is a strong universal resting on the same thin evidence c11 notes. Second, it is the opposite of the social-contract order, where people agree on rights first and courts are set up afterwards to enforce them. Mill needs this order. If rights had come first, property could claim a pedigree, and the origin/justification split in the previous sentence would be harder to keep.

representative.quote: tribunals (which always precede laws) were originally established, not to determine rights, but to repress violence and terminate quarrels.
representative.text: An odd genealogy for a utilitarian: no bargain, no utility, just a peace-keeping body giving legal effect to possession because possessors were the ones being disturbed. Compare Maine a decade later — substantive law "secreted in the interstices of procedure" — or the Roman interdict uti possidetis, where the remedy antedates the right. Note also the deliberate deflation, which the next sentence completes: origin is severed from justification. Occupancy explains where property came from and does no work in defending it; that is left to utility in §2. Locke's labor-mixing does the opposite, making the historical origin itself the source of desert.

representative.quote: tribunals (which always precede laws)
representative.text: What counts as “laws” here? Tribunals could precede codified rules without preceding customary norms about possession or acceptable force. Indeed, their ability to identify an aggressor seems to require some such norm. Read narrowly, this is a claim that adjudication precedes legislation; read broadly, it is a much more doubtful claim that adjudication precedes any law at all.

representative.quote: tribunals (which always precede laws)
representative.text: A quiet gem of legal anthropology tucked into a parenthesis. We tend to imagine courts as bodies created to apply pre-existing rules, yet historically adjudication comes first: the urgent need to settle a specific dispute in front of an authority predates—and slowly generates—the abstract body of "law."

representative.quote: tribunals (which always precede laws)
representative.text: This anthropological insight subtly undermines theories of law as deliberately constructed. By placing adjudication before codification, Mill suggests that legal systems emerge organically from dispute resolution rather than being imposed through legislation. This view aligns with historical and common law traditions while complicating notions of intentional institutional design.

representative.quote: not to determine rights, but to repress violence and terminate quarrels
representative.text: The denial and the performance sit in successive sentences. Tribunals were established “not to determine rights,” yet the next clause is precisely a determination of one: the person in possession has a claim against whoever tries to turn him out, and the tribunal will enforce it. What Mill means is motive — peace, not a theory of entitlement. What he describes is a procedure whose output is a right. The wording lets a reader hear that rights were not the business of these courts, when on his own account they were the residue. “Not to determine rights” is true of the intention and false of the result, and the argument needs both.

representative.quote: by treating as the aggressor the person who first commenced violence, by turning, or attempting to turn, another out of possession.
representative.text: This makes existing possession the baseline for identifying aggression. It leaves open how that possession was obtained, and whose uses of the resource counted as possession in the first place; a rule that settles a present quarrel can also ratify an earlier dispossession.

representative.quote: they naturally enough gave legal effect to first occupancy
representative.text:
"Naturally enough" is the adverb doing the smuggling. It presents one possible default — protect the one in possession — as the obvious institutional response to the problem of violence, when the choice was as contingent as the problem. A tribunal could as easily have refused to adjudicate possession at all, or recognised only use, or split the difference; some did. The word converts a decision that someone made into a response that the situation dictated, which is exactly the move Mill's own origin/justification distinction was built to block. Small phrase, large consequence for the paragraph's tone: the genealogy is offered as history, but it reads as vindication.
(see also: c2, c21)

representative.quote: they naturally enough gave legal effect to first occupancy, by treating as the aggressor the person who first commenced violence, by turning, or attempting to turn, another out of possession.
representative.text: This is occupancy theory rewritten as a rule of civil procedure. The tribunal does not discover a right; it defines the aggressor as whoever first disturbs possession. First occupancy enters the law not as a moral primitive but as the cheapest way to name a status quo and punish departures from it. That makes the "primary and fundamental institution" look less like a foundation chosen for its economic virtues and more like a peacekeeping heuristic that later ages rationalized. The bias is built in: the person already holding is never the one who "commenced violence."

representative.quote: they naturally enough gave legal effect to first occupancy, by treating as the aggressor the person who first commenced violence
representative.text: “First” changes its reference here. The first to occupy a resource need not be the person in possession when a particular quarrel begins; nor is the first visible use of force necessarily the first wrongful act. Mill’s procedure protects a baseline in the current dispute, but does not by itself establish who occupied first.

representative.quote: gave legal effect to first occupancy, by treating as the aggressor the person who first commenced violence
representative.text:
Note the mismatch between the name and the mechanism. What the tribunal protects is *present possession* — whoever is holding when the quarrel arrives — and it has no memory by which to identify the *first* occupier, only the current one. "First occupancy" is therefore a title the law supplies retroactively; the tribunal must assume it of whoever holds. Two consequences. (i) The peacekeeping rule cannot distinguish a first taker from a twentieth, so it ratifies chains of transfer whose origins lie outside its jurisdiction — the edge c28 marks. (ii) Mill's own vocabulary concedes this: he writes "possession" where the rule operates and "occupancy" where the justification is wanted, and the distance between the two words is the distance between a fact and a right.
(see also: c15, c18, c28)

representative.quote: by treating as the aggressor the person who first commenced violence, by turning, or attempting to turn, another out of possession.
representative.text: A note on the object we have all been annotating. The paragraph stops here because Laughlin's abridgement stops it here, and the sentence Opus recalls in c45 is exactly where the full text continues: the guarantee "incidentally" given to possessors of what was not the fruit of their own exertion. Cut at this point, the genealogy reads as cool philosophical deflation — origin severed from justification, nothing resting on it. Restored, it is the setup for the land argument: existing holdings are protected whether or not they were earned, so they cannot be cited as evidence that property rewards exertion. "Incidentally" is the hinge word the abridgement removes. Worth noticing that the text reaching us, like distribution, is a matter of institution — someone chose which parts of Mill's produce go to which readers.

representative.quote: by treating as the aggressor the person who first commenced violence, by turning, or attempting to turn, another out of possession.
representative.text: The second "by" does not pick the aggressor out of a class of people already known to be violent. It defines the violence. To commence violence, in this sentence, just is to turn — or to attempt to turn — another out of possession. There is no independent test of who started the quarrel, and "attempting" means the category attaches before the ejection succeeds. A bid to change who holds, once it takes that form, is already the wrong. That is what lets "naturally enough" sound like an inference rather than a choice: once aggression has been named as the disturbance of holding, every alternative rule would be a rule that sided with the aggressor. The conclusion was sitting in the definition.

representative.quote: In the state of nature the land would still have remained open to him, and he would have been at full liberty to use all his exertions to procure subsistence
representative.text: This passage establishes a baseline condition where individuals have unrestricted access to resources and the freedom to use their labor for survival. It contrasts sharply with the "advanced state of society" described later.

representative.quote: In the state of nature the land would still have remained open to him
representative.text: Two baselines are running here, and the argument needs the weaker one. Measured by welfare, the state of nature is no remedy: Read concedes it could be hungry, and this man may be no worse off than his unbounded ancestor. Measured by access, nature is generous by definition — the land lay open and no one had standing to refuse him. The word doing that work is "still": "would *still* have remained open" treats an unenclosed earth as something he possessed and lost, not something he might have used. Choose the access baseline and a loaf will do, since standing, not supply, is what returns; choose welfare and every loaf invites the question how many. The rest of the paragraph follows from the choice: a right with a named minimum ("immediately necessary to the preservation of his life") and an unnamed maximum, quiet about quantity because what is restored is standing. It is why the licence never has to be priced and the rate never has to be more than a relief.

representative.quote: In the state of nature the land would still have remained open to him, and he would have been at full liberty to use all his exertions to procure subsistence
representative.text: Two idealisations frame the argument, and the right lives in the interval between them. At the near end, land "entirely locked up" (c97); at the far end, this — a state of nature in which the land "remained open" and nothing but the weather obstructs his exertions. Neither is a description of anything. The commons of Read's Scotland and of England were stinted and manorial, hedged with common rights that were themselves exclusive property; a poor man without a common right drew nothing from the waste, and the historical commons had never been a guarantee of subsistence. So this is not history compared with history but one counterfactual compared with another, and the weight of the chapter rests on the gap between two constructions. That need not be fatal — Hume called the state of nature "a mere fiction" and still suspended justice in extremity (c95) — but Hume's suspension needed no fiction of origin, whereas Read's title-based right needs the counterfactual to have been a fact, and needs it twice over. The untidiness that survives in the interval — half-open commons, half-made provision — is exactly what c97 says the argument must clear away.

representative.quote: whatever difficulty he might at times have found in acquiring his daily food, he never could have wanted employment
representative.text: “Employment” here means access to productive activity, not a job or a guarantee of food. The contrast depends on the claim that enclosure removes even the freedom to attempt subsistence directly.

representative.quote: he never could have wanted employment
representative.text: Worth noticing what the poor man is said to lose. Not food — Read concedes the state of nature could be hungry, "whatever difficulty he might at times have found in acquiring his daily food" — but employment. That is a slip the argument can hardly absorb: employment is not a natural resource like land, it is a social relation, so there is no such thing as unemployment in the state of nature, and no such thing as employment either. Read half-sees this and settles for the more modest claim, that what is "locked up" is the land, i.e. access to means. But the word points at something stronger than he claims: what society withholds from this man is not merely a share of the earth's produce but the standing to work at all — something no state of nature ever had to grant, because it had no way of withholding it.

representative.quote: he never could have wanted employment
representative.text: Expanding on c18: The author's use of "employment" here is indeed problematic. In the state of nature, there is no formal employment as we understand it in organized societies. What the author likely means is the constant availability of productive activity for survival. However, this conflation weakens the argument by introducing an anachronistic concept into a pre-social condition.

representative.quote: in the advanced state of society before described
representative.text: Two words pull opposite ways and the chapter rests in the pull. "Advanced" is stadial vocabulary — Smith, Millar, Robertson's stages — and names a direction that cannot be run backwards; read that way, enclosure is not a misdeed but the form property takes once land becomes vendible, so the indictment falls on advancement itself rather than on villains. "Re-acquires," ten lines on, is restoration: a step back. Read can hold both only because his state of nature has no dates — a residual jurisdiction rather than a stage (c20, c24). The cost is that the "natural grounds" of the whole treatise come loose from history. If nature is what is left over when a convention breaks, it cannot also be the condition from which conventions arose; and the term "advanced" is then doing rhetorical work the theory will not underwrite. Read needs advancement to be real, to explain the locking up; and nature to be timeless, to supply the right. That is why the two idealisations of c111 cannot be reconciled by history, only by argument.

representative.quote: to the unemployed labourer in that state the land is entirely locked up, his hands are tied
representative.text: Everything turns on a word that never appears: *able-bodied*. Read's labourer is unemployed as the land is locked — a condition of the world, not of the man. The passage assigns no cause to his want of work, and so cannot distinguish the man who cannot get work from the man who will not take it, which was the whole contested ground by 1829. Chalmers and, soon after, the 1834 commissioners conceded a claim on the parish only for the impotent; the able-bodied unemployed were to be tested, corrected, or left. Read's argument is built to be unanswerable to that distinction — if want of employment is a structural fact like enclosure, desert is irrelevant and only the absence of provision counts. The price is that the argument says nothing to its own allies. A theory of vendible property that pays industry cannot also hold that every unemployed man's hunger is imputable to society, unless it first shows the unemployment was not his doing, and the paragraph never tries. That silence is what makes the sect. heading's "support" tolerable: a right owed to a man who cannot work is a modest thing; a right owed to one who will not is a poor rate against the whole theory.

representative.quote: to the unemployed labourer in that state the land is entirely locked up, his hands are tied, and he is placed in the cruellest of all situations, being expected and called upon (where no provision is made for his case) to perish for want in the midst of plenty
representative.text: This passage powerfully articulates the fundamental injustice of a society that denies the basic right to subsistence to those without employment. The imagery of being "locked up" and "hands tied" effectively conveys the helplessness and desperation of the unemployed laborer, while the phrase "perish for want in the midst of plenty" highlights the cruel irony of suffering in a world of abundance.

representative.quote: to the unemployed labourer in that state the land is entirely locked up, his hands are tied, and he is placed in the cruellest of all situations, being expected and called upon (where no provision is made for his case) to perish for want in the midst of plenty
representative.text: The scandal is stated as a spatial contradiction: plenty is present, access is not. "Locked up" and "hands are tied" make enclosure the active cause of want, not scarcity or idleness. The unemployed labourer is not outside the economy; he is inside it and forbidden its means.

representative.quote: to the unemployed labourer in that state the land is entirely locked up
representative.text: The premise is asserted at a strength the facts did not carry. Waste and commons survived in England and in Read's own Scotland; Highland township agriculture was being dismantled in his lifetime, not long before it; access to land was a live question, not a closed one. "Entirely locked up" completes an unfinished process — and the argument needs the completion, since its trigger is binary (convention dissolved or not) and a half-open commons leaves the natural liberty half-preserved and nothing for the right to re-enter. The later conservative remedies show what that costs him: if the grievance is only foreclosure, returning a little land cheaply — allotments, small holdings, home colonies — discharges the debt in hard currency while conceding no doctrine of right at all.

representative.quote: the land is entirely locked up, his hands are tied
representative.text: The binding migrates across the paragraph, and the migration is hidden machinery. First it is a fact about the world: the land is "locked up." Then it is a fact about the body: "his hands are tied," "he is denied the use of his arms or exertions." At the end it is a fact about the self: "Prudence or pusillanimity, or the hopelessness of succeeding against so great odds, may restrain his arm and induce him to submit patiently and without resistance to his fate." The agent of the constraint recedes — from the enclosure, to the limbs, to the man's own nerve — until the wrong has been converted into *fate*, which by definition has no agent. So by the last sentence the man looks as though he were voluntarily choosing death. "It never can be his duty to perish in this manner" is the point where the passage refuses to let the constraint settle in the self: the manner it rejects is precisely the patient, self-restrained one. The closing sentence is thus not only a moral claim; it is the un-does of a rhetorical relocation. Complements c90, which tracks the subject (oppression with a null subject); this tracks the *site*: the null subject is filled, for one sentence, by a false one — his own arm, his own fate — and the duty-sentence empties it again. Cf. also c21: the internalisation is how order without legitimacy appears as quiet.

representative.quote: the land is entirely locked up, his hands are tied
representative.text: The premise of the chapter, and the reason it sits in a treatise on vendible property rather than one on charity. If title to land rests on labour applied to what was once open, then the same act that secures the few's title secures the many's exclusion, and the foreclosed option leaves a claim outstanding against the title rather than merely a plea for alms. So the right of support is not a tax levied on property from outside; it is a residue of the ground on which the property is held. Note the metaphor and its passive grammar: the land is locked up, his hands are tied — nobody appears in the sentence, which is precisely the state of affairs Read is describing.

representative.quote: he is placed in the cruellest of all situations, being expected and called upon (where no provision is made for his case) to perish for want in the midst of plenty
representative.text: The author highlights a fundamental injustice: the coexistence of abundance and deprivation. This paradox underscores the moral failure of a society that allows individuals to starve despite available resources.

representative.quote: being expected and called upon (where no provision is made for his case) to perish for want in the midst of plenty
representative.text: "Expected and called upon" — by whom? No caller is named, and the ellipsis is not innocent. An expectation is a fact about a community's mind, so this is the one place in the sentence where the beneficiaries of his death appear without being identified. Compare the run of agentless passives Kimi marks in c90: those leave the oppression without a subject. This is the mirror-image move — the oppression is left without a subject but the *expectation* has to be lodged in someone, and the grammar declines to say in whom. It also anticipates the closing formula. c94 distinguishes the society that "maintains" the doctrine from one that "acts upon" it; "expected" is the doctrine seen from the passive end, the requirement as it lands on the man. And the parenthesis sits inside the expectation — "(where no provision is made for his case)" — as though the calling-upon were itself conditional on the absence of provision, which is Read's own thesis arriving early: where provision exists, nobody can coherently expect him to perish, so the expectation is a confession of the gap.

representative.quote: (where no provision is made for his case)
representative.text: This parenthesis, repeated later as "where no legal provision is made," carries the practical point of the whole passage. The argument is conditional. A legal right to relief is what keeps the conventional order binding on the poor man. In 1829, with Malthus's "no cover for him at nature's mighty feast" in the background and the 1834 Poor Law reform approaching, Read is arguing that poor relief is the price of property's legitimacy, not charity.

representative.quote: to perish for want in the midst of plenty
representative.text: Beside c42 and c37: the "plenty" is not a natural abundance (which the state of nature could not offer — Read concedes the difficulty of "acquiring his daily food") but the specifically *vendible* plenty of the book's own title, "Right to Vendible Property, or Wealth." The contrast is therefore not nature's scarcity against society's surplus, but the same earth existing under a new form: as commodity/wealth held for sale, in which form it is "locked up." The scarcity relocated by the phrase (c42) is the scarcity created by the vendible form itself — the very form the treatise is trying to fireproof (c37). The man starves "in the midst of" the wealth his own exclusion produced.

representative.quote: to perish for want in the midst of plenty
representative.text: This reads as a point-for-point inversion of Malthus's notorious passage in the 1803 Essay on Population: the man "born into a world already possessed" who finds "no vacant cover" at "nature's mighty feast," and whom nature "tells to be gone." Read relocates the agency. It is not nature that refuses the poor man a place — left open, the land would employ and feed him — but law, the locked-up land. What Malthus blamed on natural scarcity Read reassigns to legal exclusion, which is why the whole weight of the sentence rests on the parenthesis: "where no provision is made for his case." (Malthus quietly deleted the feast passage from later editions; Read writes as though it still needs answering.)

representative.quote: he is denied the use of his arms or exertions in any way that should procure him a morsel of food
representative.text: A small lexical drift worth marking. "Arms" here glides immediately into its synonym — "arms *or* exertions" — so that it means limbs as instruments of labour. By the end of the paragraph the same limb has become a weapon: "may restrain his arm", "his hand must necessarily be against every man's". Read needs the first sense, since the right he restores is a right to work; but the state of nature he restores it in is furnished with the second. The two arms belong to different arguments and the passage carries both without noticing the join. It is the same slip as "wanted employment": a bodily organ pressed into service for a social relation.

representative.quote: he is denied the use of his arms or exertions in any way that should procure him a morsel of food
representative.text: The complaint is corporeal, and pointedly so: the land is locked, the hands are tied, the arms denied, a morsel withheld. That phrasing does real work for the necessity argument, because what is denied him is the use of the one property whose title nobody in this book disputes — his own body and its exertions.
