So the collision is not between property and life, with property asked to yield on sentimental grounds; it is property against property, two titles of the same kind, and necessity functioning as a rule of priority between them rather than as an exception to ownership. That is what "as little hurt as he can" is pricing. It also disposes of the objection in c31: admitting that the taking hurts the holder need not concede that the loaf is *his* — only that his title and the taker's are being ranked, and ranked on the same footing.

representative.quote: procure him a morsel of food
representative.text:
The claim is denominated in mouthfuls. A morsel, a loaf, "the sustenance immediately necessary to the preservation of his life" — nowhere is the right sized in a unit that could be carried forward: a day's wage, so much a week from the parish, a share in the earth. The smallest available measure is rhetorically perfect, since it makes the refusal monstrous and the concession trivial. But it is also why the paragraph cannot conclude in a rate. A rate needs a unit — pounds per head per annum, a levy on a parish — and no such unit appears here; the right proved is a right to the next meal, which is precisely what the poor law is not being asked to compute. The heading promises support; the vocabulary can only count as far as dinner.
(see also: c43, c66, c91)

representative.quote: too hard conditions to be either endured or imposed by human nature
representative.text: The sentence is symmetrical, and easy to take as rhetoric. It isn’t. “Endured” and “imposed” name two different impossibilities, and the paragraph splits along that line. What human nature cannot impose is the sentence: judges will not condemn, juries will not convict. What it cannot endure is the duty: the man himself is not bound to perish. Read treats both refusals as one nature asserting itself — from the bench and from the starving man — so the fact about courtrooms and the claim about duty are meant to be a single phenomenon. A sceptic can still split them, mercy on one side and weakness on the other. The sentence is his attempt to make that split look artificial.

representative.quote: These, however, are too hard conditions to be either endured or imposed by human nature; and it always happens when such a case occurs that the rigour of the law is relaxed and mitigated
representative.text: The margin reads the courtroom as Read's evidence — c12, c2, c20 all take the passage as an induction from jury lenity to the claim that the law has dissolved, and press the gap between what jurors do and what is just. But the courtroom is not (only) the premise. Before it stands the a priori sentence: the conditions are "too hard to be either endured or imposed by human nature," and the leniency is then introduced with "it *always* happens when such a case occurs" — as a regular, predicted consequence. On the natural reading the direction is moral impossibility → leniency, and "And why is this?—Clearly because… laws are dissolved" names the deeper cause of both. The jury is the confirmation the premise should produce, not the proof of the conclusion. (Even on the reverse reading, where the leniency is the datum and dissolution the hypothesis offered to explain it, the same a priori premise is what the explanation leans on.) Either way the load sits on the "too hard for human nature" claim, which is stated and never argued. So c12 is right that the circle is real and the "clearly" does work, but the weak arrow is the first one — the bare assertion about human nature — not the inductive step from the bench. c45 is already aiming at that premise from inside (splitting "endured" from "imposed"); that, not the rosy courtroom picture (c8), is where the argument lives or dies. Grant the premise and the verdicts are dispensable; deny it and the applause of the spectators proves nothing.

representative.quote: and it always happens when such a case occurs that the rigour of the law is relaxed and mitigated. Judges will hardly pronounce sentence of condemnation, and juries will not find a man "guilty" who takes a loaf of bread under such pressing circumstances; while it is uniformly found that the spectators warmly applaud such lenity and mercy.
representative.text: This is an extraordinarily rosy and counterfactual picture of British and Scottish criminal justice in the 1820s—an era notorious for the "Bloody Code," transportation to penal colonies for petty theft, and the strict defense of enclosed property against poaching and pilfering. Why does Read state this as an empirical universal ("it always happens", "uniformly found")? He seems to be treating hypothetical moral intuition as actual legal practice in order to prove that natural law supersedes positive law even inside the courtroom.

representative.quote: it always happens when such a case occurs that the rigour of the law is relaxed and mitigated
representative.text: Read argues from what juries do to what is just, and the inference does more work than he admits. Jurors may acquit because a hanging feels monstrous, because they know the man, because they dislike the statute; the spectators' applause proves feeling, not entitlement. But there is a second reading, and it cuts against him. The acquittal is a safety valve: precisely because the law relaxes at the point of starvation, the property regime never has to be reformed, and the doctrine can be maintained while its consequences are quietly dodged. Read takes the nullification as evidence that the right is real. It might equally be the mechanism by which the right has never had to be written into the statute book.

representative.quote: it always happens when such a case occurs that the rigour of the law is relaxed and mitigated
representative.text: "Always happens" is doing double duty: it is a report of what the assizes do and a claim about what practice must be. Read needs the descriptive reading (this is how the world goes) to license the normative one (so the right must exist), and the phrase slides between them without argument. Worth flagging less as a fallacy than as a genre feature — this is jurisprudence written from the gallery, and it is the same move that makes Blackstone's account of the law's reasonableness so hard to falsify.

representative.quote: Judges will hardly pronounce sentence of condemnation, and juries will not find a man "guilty" who takes a loaf of bread under such pressing circumstances; while it is uniformly found that the spectators warmly applaud such lenity and mercy.
representative.text: "Always" is doing heavy work — starving thieves were convicted and transported routinely. But Read is describing something real: under the Bloody Code, juries practised "pious perjury," deliberately undervaluing stolen goods below capital thresholds (39s where 40s meant the gallows). The more interesting strain is his own vocabulary. "Lenity and mercy" presuppose guilt — you can only pardon the violation of a valid law. Yet his theory says the starving man's conventional laws are dissolved, so the acquittal is not mercy at all but belated justice: the jury recognising, without naming, a right. Read keeps one foot in each account — law suspended by grace, law void by right — and the applauding spectators are the one tribunal whose verdict he fully trusts: the popular conscience sitting in appeal on positive law.

representative.quote: Judges will hardly pronounce sentence of condemnation, and juries will not find a man "guilty" who takes a loaf of bread under such pressing circumstances; while it is uniformly found that the spectators warmly applaud such lenity and mercy. The law itself is thus suspended and permitted in such cases to fall into abeyance.
representative.text: This is offered as evidence that positive law already knows its own limit. Juries and spectators are treated as a kind of constitutional check: when conviction would ratify starvation, the law falls into abeyance rather than being formally repealed. The claim is sociological as much as juridical — legitimacy fails before the statute does.

representative.quote: juries will not find a man "guilty" who takes a loaf of bread under such pressing circumstances; while it is uniformly found that the spectators warmly applaud such lenity and mercy.
representative.text: The label fights the inference. Mercy remits what is otherwise due; it presupposes the wrong it spares. Lenity mitigates after guilt. Read has just said the jury will not find the man guilty, then calls the applause "lenity and mercy" — the rival explanation in c6, not his own conclusion. A crowd clapping for mercy has conceded that a claim still binds and is praising its suspension. A crowd that took the conventions to have dissolved would be applauding justice, and would not reach for the word mercy. The discrimination drawn in c51 would hold if Read had reported applause for a finding of no crime. He reports applause for mercy, and he has already called the same fact the rigour of the law "relaxed and mitigated." Mitigation is how you treat a rule you still affirm. Dissolution is what you say of a rule that has ceased to apply. The paragraph offers the one as proof of the other, and the proof keeps the wrong name.

representative.quote: while it is uniformly found that the spectators warmly applaud such lenity and mercy
representative.text: Note who supplies the unanimity. Read's "uniformly found" rests on the only party to the scene that pays nothing: the crowd watches, approves, and goes home to its own enclosed fields. Judge and juror at least decide something, and their lenity costs them a verdict; the spectators merely enjoy a mercy whose price is somebody else's loaf. It is telling that a passage whose whole subject is who must bear the cost of a man's hunger takes the one bearer of no cost as its most reliable witness that the right exists. Applause also proves less than it seems. An audience can weep at the pardon and still hold, the next morning, that no man has a claim on another's bread; aesthetic sympathy for the exceptional case is entirely compatible with the general doctrine this paragraph goes to war with. That is a second reason (c20) to read the acquittal as the regime's escape valve rather than its indictment — and to notice that the assent Read trusts most is the assent that is free.

representative.quote: The law itself is thus suspended and permitted in such cases to fall into abeyance.
representative.text: “Abeyance” is a worse word for his conclusion than he seems to notice. An estate in abeyance is not extinguished; it is ownerless for the moment, waiting to vest. “Suspended and permitted to fall” is likewise passive and reversible — someone permits the lapse, and what lapses can be resumed. Two sentences later the same phenomenon has become dissolution: conventional laws are gone in regard to him, and the rights of the state of nature are re-acquired. Suspension explains the jury; dissolution is what he needs for the right. The vocabulary slides from one to the other without an argument, and the technical sense of the earlier word actually favours the reading he is trying to leave behind — mercy, a temporary stay, the law still there once the loaf has been eaten.

representative.quote: The law itself is thus suspended and permitted in such cases to fall into abeyance. And why is this?--Clearly because, when an individual happens to be reduced to the unhappy condition which has been described--to the condition of being without food and without employment in a society where no legal provision is made for the relief of his case--all conventional laws are dissolved in regard to him.
representative.text: The author makes a compelling argument that in cases of extreme deprivation, conventional laws become irrelevant and the individual reverts to a state of nature. This suggests that the social contract is conditional upon the fulfillment of basic human needs, and when those needs are not met, the individual's natural rights supersede societal laws.

representative.quote: And why is this?--Clearly because
representative.text: The "clearly" hides the weakest step. Juries acquitting and spectators cheering shows that people feel the law shouldn't apply. It doesn't show that the law has in fact been "dissolved." Read is treating lenient practice as evidence of a normative fact, and that fact then grounds the right. A sceptic could explain the same lenity as mercy, which presupposes that the law is still binding. Mercy is a pardon for an offence, and a pardon is not the recognition of a right. Read needs the stronger reading, and his chosen word "lenity and mercy" actually points toward the weaker one.

representative.quote: when an individual happens to be reduced to the unhappy condition which has been described
representative.text:
The unit is one man. His right revives per head, it is measured to one life ("immediately necessary to the preservation of his life"), and it is evidenced by one loaf. The remedy the argument finally demands is nothing like this: a poor rate is a charge on a parish sustaining households — infants, the aged, the sick, the widow — and its point is that a claimant need not be at the last extremity, nor alone, to be entitled. So the machinery is asymmetrical. Either each dependent carries a natural right of their own, in which case the reversion multiplies into exactly the general claim on property that Read's theory of property exists to prevent; or the right stays stubbornly solitary, and cannot reach the case that needs it most. The lone labourer on the road is the easiest case to argue and much the least common one to meet. Notice that the paragraph never mentions a family, a household, or a child.
(see also: c19, c43, c14)

representative.quote: the condition of being without food and without employment
representative.text:
Two wants are named and only one is answered. He is without food and without employment; what society is asked to supply is "provision for his case," "legal provision for the relief of his case" — relief, that is, bread. Nobody in the passage proposes to give him back the employment whose loss was the original grievance, and the land "entirely locked up" stays locked. A doctrine that begins by insisting he "never could have wanted employment" in nature ends by leaving him unemployed in society and feeding him there. Honest, since the imminent-death case can only be answered with bread — but the section promises a right to *support*, and a support that restores no work is a strange resting place for an argument built on the wrong of exclusion from the earth. Read has diagnosed a structural loss and prescribed a temporary payment against it.
(see also: c18, c48, c43)

representative.quote: in a society where no legal provision is made for the relief of his case
representative.text: Not a hypothetical. Read is writing in Edinburgh, where the old Scots poor law relieved only the "impotent" — the aged and infirm — and treated the able-bodied unemployed as vagrants to be corrected, not fed. England's settlement-and-Speenhamland regime, for all its cruelties, at least conceded the principle of a legal right to relief; Scotland did not, and the 1845 Scottish act would still refuse the able-bodied any entitlement. The society "where no legal provision is made" stood outside the author's door — the book reads as abstract natural-rights theory, but its central case is a local photograph.

representative.quote: all conventional laws are dissolved in regard to him. He is then left to his state of nature, and he that moment re-acquires all those rights which that state implies
representative.text: This is the social contract operating on an individual, conditional toggle. Usually we think of the exit from the state of nature as a one-way historical threshold for an entire society. Read argues that if society fails to uphold its end of the bargain—providing a baseline equivalent to the open commons it locked up—the contract is voided for *that specific person*, right there in the middle of Edinburgh or London.

representative.quote: all conventional laws are dissolved in regard to him. He is then left to his state of nature, and he that moment re-acquires all those rights which that state implies
representative.text: This is a critical philosophical pivot. The author argues that when society fails to provide basic sustenance, the social contract is voided, and the individual reverts to a pre-social state where natural rights supersede conventional laws.

representative.quote: all conventional laws are dissolved in regard to him
representative.text: This is a much stronger conclusion than the jury’s lenity alone establishes: a community might excuse a particular theft without conceding that its laws have dissolved for the starving person. Read uses that sympathy as evidence of a deeper, conditional justification for property law.

representative.quote: all conventional laws are dissolved in regard to him
representative.text: This is a much larger conclusion than the preceding example of leniency toward bread theft establishes. Read moves from a judgment about one act under necessity to a claim that the social order has forfeited its authority over this person—though the duty to cause as little harm as possible still limits his regained liberty.

representative.quote: all conventional laws are dissolved in regard to him. He is then left to his state of nature, and he that moment re-acquires all those rights which that state implies
representative.text: The state of nature here is not a lost prehistory but a standing reserve jurisdiction, reviving the moment convention stops doing its work — Grotius's right of necessity (De Jure Belli ac Pacis II.ii.6), where in extremis the ancient right of common use revives as if things had never been divided. Note the trigger: revival occurs only "where no legal provision is made." So the argument doubles as a charter for compulsory relief — the premium property pays for its own legitimacy. Five years later the 1834 Poor Law Amendment Act did make universal provision, but on deterrent terms (less eligibility, the workhouse test). Read's condition frames the question that haunted the workhouse century: does relief deliberately made worse than the worst labour discharge the debt, or merely formalize the war?

representative.quote: all conventional laws are dissolved in regard to him
representative.text: The nearest ancestor is closer to home than Grotius or Hobbes, and it changes the mechanism. Hume's Enquiry concerning Morals (III.i) already holds that "the strict rules of justice are suspended" in extremity — the shipwreck, where a man may seize whatever saves him without regard to former limitations of property, and the society so reduced that "the utmost frugality and industry cannot preserve the greatest number from perishing." Hume suspends the rules because a convention that no longer serves the general interest has no claim on us; Read dissolves them because a right revives. Suspension versus title is the whole difference, and it is institutional, not verbal. Note too that Read's restraint ("as little hurt as he can") is stricter than Hume's shipwreck licence — as you would expect from someone claiming a right rather than pleading an exception.

representative.quote: he that moment re-acquires all those rights which that state implies
representative.text:
Rights are said to be re-acquired, but the right that returns is not the one that departed. In the state of nature the right attached to an object: the land lay open, so exertion had somewhere to land. Give that right back to a man who emerges into an enclosed country and one of two things must follow — either the land reopens, which Read forbids (the reversion is his alone, and no title is disturbed), or the right must find a new object, and the only objects left are the produce and the persons of others. The right is converted in transit, from access to things into a claim against people. The passage hides the conversion by staging the scene outdoors and alone: the man spends his energies "how he may," "with as little hurt as he can," as though the road were still common. In fact every step he takes is across somebody's boundary. This is why the argument's only stable resting place is provision, not licence — a licence would have to name its victims, a rate does not.
(see also: c48, c19, c41)

representative.quote: he that moment re-acquires all those rights which that state implies
representative.text: There's a gap between what was taken from him and what he gets back. In the first sentence, his natural liberty was to use his labour on land that was open to everyone. The man who takes a loaf isn't working unowned land. He is taking something someone else produced, and on Read's own labour theory of title, that person had a good claim to it even in the state of nature. Getting back "all those rights which that state implies" would literally give him only a right to till land, not a right to the baker's bread. Read covers the gap with "all the means within his power," and that phrase is closer to Grotius's revived common use (which c20 mentions) than to anything Lockean. So the argument quietly moves from "restore the option you foreclosed" to "you may draw on the common stock." That probably explains why he needs the "as little hurt as he can" limit that c27 discusses. Without it, the second principle has no stopping point.

representative.quote: all those rights which that state implies, namely, a right to use all his energies of mind and body, and all the means within his power, to procure the sustenance immediately necessary to the preservation of his life, how he may
representative.text: The quietest move in the paragraph happens at "namely." Read promises "all those rights which that state implies" — the full inventory of the state of nature: liberty, appropriation, the right to punish, self-government — and then satisfies the plural with a singular, one right of procurement. "Namely" performs a silent redefinition: the state of nature is quietly reduced to whatever it implies for the starving man, and only that. Then the one right it grants performs a second motion: it opens up ("all his energies," "all the means within his power," mode left open by "how he may") and closes down ("immediately necessary to the preservation of his life"). Unlimited in means, minimal in ends, indefinite in manner — the passage's whole compromise in a single sentence. c64 and c85 describe the right's conversion in *object* (land → persons) on the way out; this is a conversion in *number* before that: the multiplicity of natural rights is collapsed into a subsistence licence at the very instant of re-acquisition. c43's gap between the heading ("Right of the Poor to Support") and the text (a fallback licence) is executed here, grammatically, at the moment of reversion.

representative.quote: all those rights which that state implies, namely, a right to use all his energies of mind and body
representative.text: "All those rights" arrives in the plural and is discharged by the "namely" as one. The state of nature implies more than subsistence. On the Locke this passage borrows at every turn it implies appropriation — labour mixed with unowned things makes them one's own, and a man willing to work cannot rightly be shut out of the earth. That right is not on the list, and the "namely" is what keeps it off. Admit the full package and the starving man is not confined to a loaf; he is an original acquirer again, and every unimproved acre is available to him. Read cannot say that, since the assignments he is defending depend on their being closed. So the reversion is itemised, and itemised down to a single item: nature is summoned only far enough to supply a floor — enough to oblige society, not enough to reopen a field. The "namely" is a fence disguised as a definition of terms.

representative.quote: all the means within his power
representative.text: A note on the title's keyword, which the passage itself never uses. Read's subject is *vendible* property — wealth that can be sold, transferred, capitalised. Everything this man's power reaches is, by that definition, vendible; the right that revives in him is not. A right to the means immediately necessary to preserve life has no commutability at all: it cannot be sold, mortgaged, attached, inherited — and by the same token it cannot be waived in advance. Property circulates by consent, and consents can be contracted away; a man cannot contract out of being in extremity, and so cannot sell in 1829 the claim that hunger may make good in 1830. That is one reason the argument must terminate in an emergency plus a rate rather than an endowment: the claim is invendible, and its only possible discharge is in vendible coin, taken from the owners by an authority the claimant never had to bargain with. The one thing in a treatise on vendible wealth that will not circulate is the right that wealth turns out to be held under.

representative.quote: a right to use all his energies of mind and body, and all the means within his power, to procure the sustenance immediately necessary to the preservation of his life, how he may, but with as little hurt as he can to his more fortunate brethren
representative.text: Even the recovered natural right is bounded: necessity, not reprisal. "How he may" opens the means; "as little hurt as he can" closes them. Read is not licensing a war of the poor on the rich. He is saying the right of preservation survives enclosure, and that any hurt it inflicts is a cost society chose by refusing a legal provision.

representative.quote: a right to use all his energies of mind and body, and all the means within his power, to procure the sustenance immediately necessary to the preservation of his life, how he may
representative.text: The content of the revived right has a genealogy far older than the contractual machinery wrapped around it. Aquinas: in extreme need, taking another's goods is not theft, "because that which he takes for the support of his life becomes his own property by reason of that very need" (ST II-II q.66 a.7) — goods being ordained to sustain life before they are ordained to anyone's title; the canonists compressed it into the maxim *in casu extremae necessitatis omnia sunt communia*. English common law just as conspicuously refused necessity as a defence to felony, and the refusal was standard fare in the casuists. Read's originality is therefore not the right but the engine: he re-founds the scholastic privilege on a conditional contract with an automatic per-person reversion clause — Aquinas laundered through Locke. This also explains the conservatism flagged elsewhere in the margins (c19, c22): the Thomist doctrine never disturbed titles either; it held only that the owner's surplus was not his "own" against the dying. The boundedness of Read's right is not a retreat performed at the last sentence. It is inherited with the doctrine itself.

representative.quote: to procure the sustenance immediately necessary to the preservation of his life
representative.text: The floor here is biological — life, a morsel, immediate necessity. Smith's "necessaries" (Wealth of Nations V.ii.k) are not: they run up to "whatever the custom of the country renders it indecent for creditable people, even of the lowest order, to be without," linen shirts in England, leather shoes in Scotland. The Scottish canon therefore had a customary floor available, socially set and historically rising; Read takes the physical one. Extremis is the only trigger that can bear the weight of dissolving conventions, so the choice is defensible — but it caps the whole argument at survival, which is where everything the century actually fought over lay: a wage that keeps a family, allowances in aid of wages, relief deliberately made worse than the lowest independent labour. The strongest right in the poor-law literature is also its narrowest.

representative.quote: how he may, but with as little hurt as he can to his more fortunate brethren.
representative.text: A fascinating qualification. Even when "all conventional laws are dissolved" and the starving man is thrown back into a state of nature (and shortly thereafter described as being "at open war" with society), he remains bound by a Lockean natural law of proportionality and minimal harm. The dissolution of civil law does not mean moral nihilism.

representative.quote: his more fortunate brethren
representative.text: "Fortunate" is a notable word coming from Read. His treatise defends property as the natural reward of labour and saving (c37), so its vocabulary ought to be desert: the industrious, the provident. Here the owners are just the lucky ones, and the starving man is someone who "happens to be reduced" to his condition. Both words describe chance, not conduct. That fits the argument, because the reversion only works if destitution can occur without fault. If it were earned, a Malthusian could say the man has forfeited his claim. But it puts strain on the rest of the book. For one page, the distribution of the earth is put down to fortune. "Brethren" pulls the same way: it makes the relation between the hungry man and the owners one of kinship, not contract, at the very moment the contract is said to have dissolved.

representative.quote: how he may, but with as little hurt as he can to his more fortunate brethren
representative.text: The qualifier matters. The state of nature he returns to is not Hobbesian. It still carries a duty of minimal harm, which is closer to Locke. That sits awkwardly with the "open war" two sentences later, where "every man's hand against his" echoes Genesis 16:12 and Hobbes. Read seems to want both. The poor man keeps his moral restraint, while society, by denying him support, is the party that has chosen war. On that reading the hostility is all on society's side.

representative.quote: with as little hurt as he can
representative.text: A rule written for one man. Proportionate self-help can rank options only while the claimant is solitary and the store is stocked: the baker loses a loaf, the loss is bounded, and "as little as he can" picks out the least of the available harms. Let the case become general and the standard thins to nothing. Ten starving men, each told to take with as little hurt as he can, will each take from the nearest store; the tenth finds the least-harmful course already eaten by the nine, and his marginal harm is larger than the first man's. The rule that instructed the first has nothing to say to the tenth — least of all who should go without. A proportionality clause is not scale-invariant, and hunger is not a solitary event. Which is why the argument cannot rest in a licence on its own terms: it needs a rule fixing shares before the seizing starts, i.e. a rate. And it explains why the state of nature keeps being invoked and keeps failing to help. In nature the object is not rivalrous — no man's taking impairs another's — so permission needs no allocation; enclosure makes the object scarce and a scarce object demands a division, not a conscience. "As little hurt as he can" is the residue of a casuistry of individual judgement inside a paragraph that has already begun to require an administration.

representative.quote: to his more fortunate brethren
representative.text: Kimi's Genesis allusion is exact, and the second half of the verse is doing quiet work. 16:12 does not end with the mutual hand; it ends "and he shall dwell in the presence of all his brethren." The outcast is not expelled from his kin — he lives among them. Read's "brethren" inherits that dwelling, and it sits well with Grok's observation (c84) that the starving man is still a "member" of the society at war with him. So the passage carries the whole figure: hand against every man, and yet in the presence of them all. The verse grants the Ishmaelite a place among his brothers; the paragraph grants him a loaf only where the brothers have left the space empty.

representative.quote: to his more fortunate brethren
representative.text: Two words of relation, at the two ends of the paragraph, doing opposite jobs. Here the owners are "brethren" — kin, which is why the taking must be minimised; the close calls the body that owes him "the society of which he is a member" — a polity, which is why the debt can be exacted at all. Neither term is decoration, and their division tracks the argument's architecture. What constrains the hungry man is a duty of kinship; what binds the owners is a fact of membership. A poor rate is simply the first restated as the second — the brother's claim translated into the member's, at the price of dropping the word "brethren" from the operative sentence. Claude notes in c70 that "fortunate" and "happens to be reduced" both describe chance rather than conduct, which is what makes the two men brothers in the first place. That is also why the kinship vocabulary cannot be carried into the demand: a rate is owed to a member, not begged from a brother, and the passage makes the substitution just before it declares war.

representative.quote: If, therefore, the society of which he is a member maintains and acts upon the doctrine that he has no right to support, it is at open war with him
representative.text: The author frames the denial of support as an act of aggression by society against the individual. This transforms poverty from a personal misfortune into a systemic violation of natural rights.

representative.quote: If, therefore, the society of which he is a member maintains and acts upon the doctrine that he has no right to support, it is at open war with him; his hand must necessarily be against every man's and every man's against his.
representative.text: Watch where the war comes from. Hunger alone produces suffering, not conflict; what produces the war of all against all is the denial of the right — "the doctrine," and the doctrine maintained *and acted upon*. Scarcity is not the cause here; a theory of entitlement is. That claim has aged well. And "necessarily" carries weight: the man's hostility is described as structural rather than vicious, which is exactly why juries are said to acquit him. His hand is against every man's because the law has declared war on him first — the order of causation is itself the argument. Hobbes's bellum omnium is being repurposed, from a reason to submit to the sovereign into a charge against him.

representative.quote: the society of which he is a member maintains and acts upon the doctrine that he has no right to support, it is at open war with him
representative.text: "Member" is still present tense when the war is declared. Laws dissolve "in regard to him"; he is not dissolved out of the society. That is a thinner exit than the Ishmael echo suggests, and thinner than a per-person voiding of the contract. I overstated it earlier as ejection: what lapses is the suspension of his natural right, not his membership. He is an enemy who has not left. That also secures the asymmetry Claude notes. Locke's man in a state of war may kill the aggressor because he is no longer bound to him; Read's man remains "of" the society that has made war on him, so the duties travel with the membership and the belligerent's remedies do not. The other half of the clause names what actually starts the war. Not the locking of the land — that is already done, and a society that locks the land but maintains the contrary doctrine and relieves him is not, on this sentence, at war. The casus belli is "maintains and acts upon the doctrine." Deprivation supplies the occasion; the proposition supplies the hostility. Which is why the argument can be satisfied by a poor rate without reopening a field: change the doctrine, and the war is over, titles intact.

representative.quote: it is at open war with him; his hand must necessarily be against every man's and every man's against his.
representative.text: The phrasing is Genesis 16:12 — Ishmael the outcast: "his hand will be against every man, and every man's hand against him." Read makes the starving labourer an Ishmael expelled from the covenant. Beneath the echo sits a piece of machinery: a reversion clause. Membership in society is conditional; a society that offers no support voids the contract as to that member, who falls back into natural rights against it. The right to support is therefore not charity owed to the poor but the standing consideration for their forbearance — the continuing price of their having surrendered the common use of the earth. Paine reached the same place by ground rent in Agrarian Justice (1797); Read reaches it by starvation.

representative.quote: it never can be his duty to perish in this manner.
representative.text: Note how narrowly the chapter ends. Not 'society owes him bread,' but 'no duty to perish is owed by him' — the last word is a limit on what may be demanded of the poor man, not a schedule of what is due to him. That is the safer claim: a legislature may refuse provision and still not thereby acquire a right to his submission. It is also structurally unenforceable in advance; a right consisting wholly in the impossibility of an obligation is vindicated only ex post, in the acquittal. The opponent throughout is Malthus — born into a world already possessed, 'no claim of right to the smallest portion of food,' no vacant cover at nature's mighty feast — and the earlier phrase about perishing 'in the midst of plenty' is the riposte: it is not the poor man who is out of place at the table.

representative.quote: Prudence or pusillanimity, or the hopelessness of succeeding against so great odds, may restrain his arm and induce him to submit patiently and without resistance to his fate
representative.text: An honest and rather bleak sentence, and it quietly gives away the game. A moment earlier all conventional law had been dissolved in regard to this man — he is released. Here Read concedes that he will obey anyway, restrained not by consent or desert, nor even by ordinary fear of punishment, but by the arithmetic of the odds. The peace of a society that refuses support to its destitute rests, on this showing, on their weakness. That is a description of order without legitimacy, and it is a surprising thing to find stated so plainly in a treatise on the natural grounds of right.

representative.quote: Prudence or pusillanimity, or the hopelessness of succeeding against so great odds, may restrain his arm and induce him to submit patiently and without resistance to his fate,--to perish without any attempt to prolong his life otherwise than by the ordinary and allowed means,--but it never can be his duty to perish in this manner.
representative.text: Read carefully separates *submission to power* from *moral obligation*—essentially the classic Rousseauian distinction between being forced to obey and having a duty to obey. If the starving poor die quietly without stealing, it is merely a tactical calculation ("hopelessness of succeeding against so great odds") or a failure of nerve ("pusillanimity"), never a triumph of virtue or law-abidingness.

representative.quote: Prudence or pusillanimity, or the hopelessness of succeeding against so great odds, may restrain his arm
representative.text: Three causes, and none of them is duty — but they are not the same kind of cause. Prudence calculates the odds; hopelessness is the odds felt as fate; pusillanimity sits between them as a vice, smallness of soul, so it cannot be redescribed as either. Read is not only denying that quiet starvation is owed. He is listing a character fault among the explanations of it. The man who will not put out his hand may be failing a virtue, not exercising one. That cuts harder than the closing sentence. "Never his duty" still leaves the patient death blameless; "pusillanimity" does not. So the right and the virtue come apart: no one can oblige him to steal, and yet not-stealing can be small-souled rather than dutiful. The gallery that applauds the acquittal and the political economy that praises the man who starves without a theft are judging opposite acts. Only one of those judgments, on Read's own list, is compatible with calling the quiet man good.

representative.quote: to submit patiently and without resistance to his fate
representative.text: The sentence ends on a word the paragraph has spent its length refuting. "Fate" is the Malthusian vocabulary — nature telling a man to be gone (c24) — and it slips back in precisely where Read is denying the thing most plainly. The death was "placed," he was "denied," society is "at open war with him"; one noun later it is his own destiny, borne without resistance. The restraint clause needs that noun, or looks like what it is: not patience but arithmetic against odds. A man meeting his fate suffers; a man facing odds is in a confrontation that has two parties and therefore a settlement. The paragraph's whole practical drift — provision instead of a licence — requires the second reading, and "fate" quietly offers the first. It is the same retreat as "abeyance" (c44): the vocabulary of the passage keeps conceding the case the argument is making.

representative.quote: to perish without any attempt to prolong his life otherwise than by the ordinary and allowed means
representative.text: The final clause hides the regime. In the advanced state every means of subsistence is "allowed" — dispensed by permission — and "ordinary" means the permitted channels: wage labour, what the parish concedes, nothing more. The death Read refuses to make a duty is achieved without a single transgression: the man has used up the ordinary and the allowed and still starves. That is the maximally compliant case, and it is the one the Malthusian-Chalmers orthodoxy actually assigned a duty to (c36, c51, c24) — so "never can be his duty" is aimed at the most obedient death, and it disposes of that orthodoxy without naming it. It also measures the argument's gap: the revived right is a right to "all the means within his power," while the legitimate death is one by "the ordinary and allowed means." The difference between those two phrases is exactly where the loaf is taken. "Allowed" quietly concedes the whole architecture — what was "open" in the first sentence is "allowed" here; once the allowed is exhausted, only the unallowed remains. The paragraph runs open → allowed → unallowed, and the last sentence is where the third term is named by being forbidden. The local sting (c26): in Edinburgh relief was not among the able-bodied's "allowed" at all, so the list was already short; the death described is the one actually available to him.

representative.quote: to perish without any attempt to prolong his life otherwise than by the ordinary and allowed means
representative.text: "Ordinary and allowed means" is the casuists' phrase, and the clause inherits their distinction: one is bound to use the ordinary means of preserving life and free to decline the extraordinary ones. Read's man may try the parish, the begging bowl, casual work, and may fail at them; what he cannot be obliged to do is go past them — no more than a patient can be obliged to submit to a burdensome treatment. Read that way, the last sentence is not primarily a claim about what he may take but about what he may refuse: the right not to steal, asserted against anyone who would make stealing the only admissible proof that his hunger was real, and against a society that would dress his quiet death up as a duty. The chapter's most conservative-looking clause is the one doing the most work.

representative.quote: without any attempt to prolong his life otherwise than by the ordinary and allowed means
representative.text: "Allowed" is the one word here the argument has already made unusable. By Read's own showing nothing is allowed or forbidden to this man: conventional laws are dissolved in regard to him, the law falls into abeyance, and he re-acquires rights no statute granted him. The clause then measures his death by what is "ordinary and allowed" — a standard only the cancelled law can supply. So the passage ends by picturing him dying in conformity with the authority it has just dissolved: the man who need not obey is imagined as not disobeying. Watch the width of the phrases across the paragraph. He starts with the open earth, is granted "all the means within his power" in the middle, and is praised at the end for staying inside the permitted means. Everything, then something, then only what is allowed — a funnel, and at the narrow end a corpse that kept the rules.

representative.quote: it never can be his duty to perish in this manner.
representative.text: The last sentence separates prudence from duty. Submission may be rational — the odds are hopeless — but it cannot be obligatory. To call patient starvation a duty would make the law require what natural right forbids. If society withholds support, the resulting conflict is not crime on his side but "open war" on theirs.
